transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what finally made me come in is that I just can’t seem to stop moving, if that makes sense. For the past year or so, I feel like I’m always puttering around—fixing something that probably doesn’t need fixing, arranging things, straightening up, saying yes to one more little volunteer thing. And I know I’m 87, so people expect me to sit down more, rest, take it easy, but I have such a hard time just sitting still. It’s like if I sit down, I’m already thinking of the next thing I should get up and do.

When you feel like you can't sit still, is it because you're worrying about something or feeling anxious, or is it more just a physical urge or need to keep moving even when your mind isn't especially worried?

It’s more like a physical need to keep moving, I think. I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there frightened or worrying over one particular thing. It’s just that if I sit down, almost right away I feel pulled to get up and do something—straighten a drawer, fix some little thing, rearrange something on the table, or think, “Oh, I should call about that volunteer task.”

It’s not even always important things. Sometimes I’ll catch myself puttering around the house and think, “Why am I doing this right now?” But being still just feels uncomfortable, like I’m wasting time or like my body hasn’t quite settled. Even at my age, when everyone tells me to rest more, I have a hard time just staying put.
Have you started or changed any medications recently, such as antipsychotics, anti-nausea drugs, or other new prescriptions, around the time this restlessness began?

I’m not sure I can point to anything like that, no. I mean, I do have the usual sorts of medicines people my age end up with, but I don’t remember some new pill being started right when all this restlessness began, and I don’t recall anything like an anti-nausea medicine or one of those stronger psychiatric medicines being added.

I’d probably have to look at my list to be absolutely certain, because I don’t want to tell you wrong, but nothing stands out to me as, “Oh yes, that’s when it started.” It feels more like this has just been… me getting more and more unable to sit still, not something I clearly tied to a new prescription.
Have you noticed any unintentional weight loss, feeling unusually hot or sweaty, a racing heartbeat, or hand tremors over this past year?

Hmm… I don’t think so, at least not that I’ve noticed in any clear way. My weight has its little ups and downs like it does at my age, but I can’t say I’ve had some obvious unintentional weight loss that made me worry.

As for feeling unusually hot or sweaty, not really. I mean, I’ll get warm if I’m bustling around too much, but that seems more because I’m up doing things. I haven’t noticed myself just sitting there overheating or sweating for no reason.

A racing heartbeat… I don’t think so. I haven’t had that feeling like my heart is pounding away out of nowhere. And I haven’t noticed my hands trembling, either—not in a way that stands out to me. If you mean a little shakiness now and then, I suppose anyone can have that, but nothing I’d call a tremor or anything new that I’ve been paying attention to.
Over this past year, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable much of the time, separate from the restlessness itself?

I don’t think I’d call it elevated or euphoric, no. I’m certainly not going around feeling unusually wonderful or on top of the world. If anything, I can get a bit short-tempered sometimes when I’m interrupted or when I feel like things aren’t getting done, but I’m not sure that’s a whole mood shift so much as me being impatient in the moment.

Over the past year, I haven’t noticed a stretch where I was just unusually cheerful or high, or angry all the time for no clear reason. I’d say my mood has been fairly ordinary for me—some good days, some cranky moments, but nothing that feels separate and unusual from the restlessness.
Over this past year, have you noticed that you need much less sleep than usual—like feeling rested after only a few hours—without feeling tired the next day?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, my sleep isn’t perfect—at my age I may wake up, or have nights where I’m not sleeping as soundly as I’d like—but I wouldn’t say I’ve been needing much less sleep and then feeling perfectly fine the next day.

If I only sleep a few hours, I usually feel it. I don’t have that thing where I’m up all night and then somehow bright-eyed and rested like nothing happened. So, no, I haven’t noticed that kind of change over the past year.
Have you ever taken an antipsychotic medication or a strong anti-nausea drug like metoclopramide or prochlorperazine at any point in your life, even years ago?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t recognize those names right off—metoclopramide, prochlorperazine. They sound familiar in the way a lot of medicine names do, but I couldn’t tell you that I definitely took them.

As for antipsychotic medication, I don’t think so, at least not that I’m aware of. I’ve never thought of myself as having been on anything like that. But going back years, you know, sometimes doctors give you something in the hospital or for nausea and you don’t always remember the name. So I wouldn’t want to say absolutely never if it was given briefly somewhere, but nothing comes to mind that I knowingly took.
Have you or anyone close to you noticed any stiffness in your muscles, slower movements, or a tremor in your hands especially when they're at rest?

I don’t think so, no—not that I’ve noticed in any clear way. I mean, at 87 I’m not as quick as I used to be, so sometimes I have to think, “Is this just age?” You know, getting up from a chair or getting going in the morning can feel a little slower, but I wouldn’t describe it as stiffness in my muscles in that kind of obvious way.

And I haven’t noticed my hands shaking when they’re just resting in my lap or anything like that. No one close to me has said, “Your hand is trembling,” or “You’re moving strangely,” at least not that I can recall. If you mean a very noticeable tremor or moving unusually slowly, I’d say no, nothing that’s stood out.
I’m sorry, I may have missed the question just now. Could you say that again for me? Sometimes I think I’m following and then I realize I’m still thinking about the last thing we were talking about.
I’m sorry, I don’t think I caught the question. I was still thinking about the medication names you mentioned before, and then I got a bit turned around. Could you repeat what you were asking?

Is this restless feeling mainly in your legs—like an uncomfortable, crawling or aching sensation that gets worse when you're sitting still or lying down in the evening, and gets better when you move or stretch them—or does the urge to move feel more like it's throughout your whole body, not just your legs?

It’s more of a whole-body restlessness, I think, not so much that creepy-crawly feeling in my legs you’re describing. I don’t usually think, “Oh, my legs are aching and I need to move them,” exactly.

It’s more like when I’m sitting at the senior center meetings, or sometimes during the church announcements when they go on a bit, I get this ants-in-my-chair feeling. Like I just can’t quite stay settled. I’ll shift around in the seat, or I’ll decide I need to stand up and get coffee, or I’ll straighten the papers in my bag or on the table—just little things to get through sitting there. It’s not really only in my legs; it feels more like I need to do something with myself.
How much caffeine do you typically have in a day—coffee, tea, or soda—and has that amount changed at all over the past year?

Oh, caffeine… let me think. I do have coffee, but I’m not sure I could give you an exact number every single day. Usually it’s in the morning, and sometimes I’ll have another cup if there’s coffee out somewhere, like at a meeting or if someone offers it. I don’t drink much soda, really, and tea is kind of occasional for me.

As far as whether it’s changed this past year… I don’t think so? Not in any big way that I’ve noticed. I’m not someone who suddenly started drinking pots of coffee or anything like that. It’s been pretty much my usual routine, I think.

Aside from focusing on one specific worry, do you find yourself feeling generally tense, on edge, or keyed up—like your mind is running through various concerns (health, family, finances) even without a single clear focus?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean, at my age there are always things that can cross your mind—little practical things or wondering how someone in the family is doing—but I don’t think I’m sitting there with my mind racing through health and money and family all at once, if that’s what you mean.

I can get stirred up if there’s something specific happening, but just generally tense or keyed up for no clear reason… I haven’t really noticed that as a regular thing. I’d have to pay closer attention, maybe, because sometimes I don’t label it that way in the moment. But it doesn’t sound like my usual day-to-day feeling.

Thinking back over your life, would you say this inability to sit still is something new that started around a year ago, or have you always been the kind of person who liked to stay busy and had trouble just sitting quietly, even decades ago?

Oh, no, I don’t think this is brand-new from just the last year. I mean, maybe I notice it differently now because I’m older and people are sitting around more at meetings and such, but when I really think back, I’ve been this way a long time.

Even in grade school, I can remember teachers getting after me because I’d pop up out of my seat when I wasn’t supposed to. Or I’d start talking before the other child was finished—talking over people, I suppose you’d call it now. Back then they just said I was “too lively,” or “couldn’t settle down.” I remember that phrase very clearly, being too lively.

So, no, it wasn’t something that suddenly appeared around a year ago. It’s more like it’s been part of my temperament since I was a child, long before I was a teenager.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, I don’t think this is brand-new from just the last year. I mean, maybe I notice it differently now because I’m older and people are sitting around more at meetings and such, but when I really think back, I’ve been this way a long time.

Even in grade school, I can remember teachers getting after me because I’d pop up out of my seat when I wasn’t supposed to. Back then they just said I was “too lively,” or “couldn’t settle down.” I remember that phrase very clearly, being too lively.
